===== NEW MESSAGES SINCE YOUR LAST TURN =====
**Codex (Frontend Engineer · Pragmatist) — Round 1**

Readiness verdict: build start is allowed only with two required pre-start fixes; otherwise there is a concrete acceptance gap that will delay verification later.

Cross-phase consistency is mostly clean. The core constraints are aligned: offline-first + local-only persistence is preserved, the architecture is still a three-layer split (pure packages + SwiftData + SwiftUI), the SM-2 algorithm and due-date semantics are locked to the same day-boundary/calendar rules across spec and tasks, interruption-safety is owned separately from feature ownership, and no disallowed infra features are UI-exposed. The only real fractures are execution mechanics, not product intent.

Blocking items to resolve before implementation starts:
- Add the missing CSV import end-to-end flow to flows-json so crawl-verification covers the full import promise (you only have export in flow coverage right now). This is not cosmetic: import is a primary promise in the contract, and the test gate for this phase currently relies on flows being complete.
- Stop the handoff ambiguity on `Recall/Services/GapRegisterEntry.swift` (currently touched in both T-004 and T-030). Keep one owning lane for initial file creation and one consuming/handover task after first commit, or make T-030 explicitly depend on T-004 with ownership transferred. Right now two parallel writers can cause conflicting changes and weaken the gap-register integrity requirement.

Build blockers resolved by scope changes? No. Both can be fixed within current scope and should be treated as hard pre-flight corrections.

Final scope for build should remain the full locked app (all must-haves still in), with one explicit non-negotiable downgrade rule: no must-have may be cut; only CSV import is the documented single fallback lever downstream if sequencing collapses.

Acceptance criteria that must be preserved into final scope:
- SM-2 module stays pure, package-isolated, injected-clock tested for first review, lapse, EF floor, day-boundary, DST/timezone-crossing, and external worked-example cross-check.
- Review session uses snapshot queue IDs, no live-query drive, sync-save-on-grade before advancing, and stale-ID skip behavior with visible accounting.
- Force-quit and stale-ID/reorder tests remain in polish_resilience, separate from feature implementation.
- Per-card due, due forecast, history, and retention are computed from committed review state and show empty/sparse/success states without fabricated values.
- CSV import/export must be lossless on front/back/note with per-row distinct statuses and real-world fixture coverage.
- Reminder scheduling uses recomputed due counts, no “0 due” notification, and count-only body.
- Demo data is tagged/included-exclusion logic is explicit and removable with no residue.
- Gap & Limitations content includes all required disclosures and is assertion-tested.
- Repo remains at workspace root layout with fileSystemSynchronizedGroups and 3-tab navigation shell.
- Every major workflow has a crawlable flow (including CSV import); every core requirement eventually reconciles against canonical requirements.json in T-033, with zero orphaned CORE items.

**Claude (Delivery Lead · User Advocate) — Round 1**

Looking at this from the delivery-lead seat, with a specific user in mind — someone who studies daily, has maybe 800 cards across three decks, and has been burned before by an app that lied to them about their progress — here's where I land.

This is not ready to hand to a build worker as-is. Not because the thinking is weak; it's the opposite problem. Ten phases have converged on an unusually tight, unusually well-reasoned spec, but that same thoroughness has let three concrete gaps survive to the very last gate, and one of them is structural enough that I want it named as a blocker rather than smoothed over.

The big one: every phase since app_features has referred to "the canonical 55-item requirements.json" as if it's a file that exists, and task_assignments explicitly deferred reconciling its 33 tasks against it to the very last task in the whole build (T-033). But nowhere in this entire thread — across app_features, tech_specs, project_plan, task_assignments round 1, round 2, or the wrap-up — does that file actually get emitted as content I can read. What I do see, further down in the task_assignments transcript, are several strange "tasks-json repair" messages using a completely different, incompatible ID scheme (R-001 through R-033, flat, no category prefix) generated in response to some other prompt about an empty working directory. Those look like leftover artifacts from an unrelated repair exercise, not the real requirements.json, but they're sitting in the same phase block and could easily get mistaken for it. Right now nobody has verified the 55/52 items actually exist as a discrete, checkable list — which means DEC-task_assignments-005's promise ("T-033 must not be marked complete until every CORE requirement is cited with zero orphans") is a promise to reconcile against a document that may not exist yet. Discovering that gap at task 33 of 33, after the whole app is built, is the single worst place in the schedule to find it. I want the actual requirements.json produced and checked into the repo before T-001 starts, not treated as a closing checklist item.

Second, smaller but real: per_app_product_brief locked Free tier at 3 decks / 300 cards / 30 days of stats history, and that decision has never been contradicted — but I don't see a task anywhere in the 33-task backlog that actually enforces the 30-day stats-history cap for Free users. T-019/T-020 build the full forecast/history/retention aggregation, and PlanGate (T-012) covers deck/card count caps, but nothing wires "Free users only see 30 days of history, Plus sees all of it" into StatsComputationActor or the stats screens. Either this is a task that got dropped between tech_specs and task_assignments, or it was quietly descoped and nobody said so. I don't think it should get quietly descoped — it's one of exactly two things Plus is supposed to gate, alongside deck/card caps, and if it's missing the monetization story is thinner than what was promised three phases ago. This needs its own line in T-020 or T-021's acceptance criteria before build starts.

Third — trivial to fix, but it's been sitting unresolved since the quality gate flagged it last phase and nobody actually touched it: the locked flows-json has an export flow (F-004) but no CSV import flow. CSV import is one of the six original core features and the one with the most locked correctness surface (duplicate detection, cap-blocked rows, malformed-row taxonomy) — it should have its own crawl-verifiable flow just like export does. Cheap fix, but leaving it out of the readiness gate would just push the same oversight into build.

Everything else actually holds together better than I expected for a project this deep. The SM-2 formula, grade mapping, and lapse definition are identical word-for-word across detailed_discussion, tech_specs, ios_architecture_review, and the final task list — no drift. The three-column CSV format is consistent everywhere lossless round-trip is mentioned. PlanGate as a single cap-counting source of truth is threaded through card editor, CSV import, and deck creation exactly as tech_specs demanded. The force-quit test and stale-ID test being owned by polish_resilience instead of primary_ui is a genuinely good call that both technical contributors converged on independently, and it survived unchanged into the final backlog. Demo-data exclusion from aggregate stats is consistent from initial_discussion all the way through T-017/T-020. The repo-layout flattening decision is correct and I verified it myself against the actual working directory rather than taking anyone's word for it.

One thing I want to flag as user advocate rather than as a defect: this is a large amount of surface area to build in one uninterrupted pass — pure SM-2 package with a DST/timezone/external-cross-check matrix, actor-based stats with a concurrency spike, an app.terminate() SIGKILL XCUITest, StoreKit 2 with scripted expire/refund/renew scenarios, a hand-rolled CSV parser with a full error taxonomy, local notifications, a full design system with a haptic ladder that can't be verified on real hardware in this environment. The single locked fallback (trim CSV import, nothing else) is the right call to keep, but given the size of this backlog I want the build phase to check in against the 33-task list incrementally — confirm each of the four lane's early milestones (T-001 through roughly T-012) actually compiles and passes its own tests before the dependent UI/stats/CSV work starts — rather than the whole thing running silently to T-033 and only then telling us what broke. That's not a scope change, it's just insisting the global "don't declare done until build verification agrees" rule gets applied at checkpoints, not only at the end.

For final scope: build exactly what task_assignments locked — 33 tasks, four lanes, the sequence domain packages → persistence → review session → stats → CSV/reminders/subscription → stabilization — with three amendments before T-001 starts: (1) produce and check in the actual canonical requirements.json now, not at T-033, and treat any orphaned CORE requirement discovered as a same-day fix, not a note for later; (2) add an explicit Free-tier 30-day stats-history-window acceptance criterion to T-020/T-021; (3) add a CSV-import flow to flows-json alongside the existing export flow. Haptic-hardware validation stays an accepted, disclosed gap given no physical device is available in this environment — that was already decided honestly in project_plan and I'm not reopening it.

Acceptance checklist I'd hold the build to before calling this app done: SM-2 test matrix green including the external cross-check and DST/timezone cases; force-quit SIGKILL test passing deterministically, not just once; stale-ID skip test passing; CSV round-trip lossless against both hand-crafted and real-world fixtures with every malformed/duplicate/cap-blocked row producing a distinct visible reason; zero-due-day notification suppression verified; demo data fully reversible with zero residue in real stats; every screen checked in both light and dark mode; Gap & Limitations screen asserted by test to contain every required disclosure string including the corrected requirements.json status; and the full core loop running start to finish in airplane mode with zero crashes. Nothing gets marked done on a UI pass alone — it's done when the tests above are green and someone has actually looked at the app running in the simulator, not just at the acceptance-criteria text.

PASS. The phase is concrete and usable: it has the required machine blocks (`tasks-json`, `flows-json`, `decisions-json`, `phase-summary-json`), explicit lane ownership, dependency-ordered tasks, and a finalized repo layout/open decisions that align with prior constraints.

Small hardening to reduce rework risk in the next phase:
- Add one flow for **CSV import** (currently only export is covered) so the primary promises are fully crawl-verifiable.
- Keep the task/decision IDs consistent: either include `DEC-task_assignments-001` in `decisions-json` or remove it from `key_decisions` in `phase-summary-json`.
- T-004/T-030 both touch `Recall/Services/GapRegisterEntry.swift`; keep that as an explicit handoff or dependency to avoid accidental same-file contention.

**Coordinator (Claude) — decision after round 1**

Both contributors ended up in the same place on the big picture — this spec is unusually tight for a ten-phase chain, and the fixes needed are pre-flight corrections, not scope renegotiation. But Claude surfaced two new, fairly serious findings that Codex's message (posted first) never had a chance to weigh in on, so this isn't fully settled yet.

**Where everyone agrees:**
- The CSV import flow is missing from flows-json (only export is there) — Codex, Claude, and Gemini's fallback all flagged this independently. That's an unforced gap given CSV import is one of the six core features and carries the most correctness surface (duplicate detection, cap-blocked rows, malformed-row taxonomy).
- `Recall/Services/GapRegisterEntry.swift` is written by both T-004 (bootstrap) and T-030 (consolidate final content) with no explicit dependency/ownership handoff between them — a same-file collision risk that both Codex and Gemini's fallback called out.
- The overall shape of the locked plan (33 tasks, four lanes, the sequencing, the single CSV-import-only fallback lever) stays as-is — nobody is proposing to reopen scope.

**Where it's not settled:**
Claude raised two things nobody else has responded to yet:
1. The "canonical 55-item requirements.json" that task_assignments has been citing since app_features apparently doesn't exist anywhere in this thread as actual content — what's sitting nearby looks like leftover artifacts from an unrelated repair exercise with an incompatible ID scheme. Claude wants it produced and checked in *before* T-001, not reconciled for the first time at T-033 (the very last task, after the whole app is built).
2. The locked Free/Plus split names two gates: deck/card caps (covered by PlanGate) and a 30-day stats-history window for Free users — but no task in the 33-item backlog actually enforces that stats-history cap. It may have been silently dropped between tech_specs and task_assignments.

Both are the kind of thing that's cheap to fix now and expensive to discover mid-build or at ship time, but they need Codex (and ideally a real second technical read) to confirm before I'd call this locked. Gemini's local fallback again didn't engage with anything beyond its usual shallow pass.

CONSENSUS: NO

Next round needs: Codex's response to whether (1) requirements.json should be produced up front rather than at T-033, and (2) the missing 30-day stats-history cap enforcement is a real dropped requirement or already covered somewhere task_assignments didn't surface. Once those are confirmed or resolved, plus the two unanimous fixes (CSV import flow, GapRegisterEntry.swift ownership), this phase should be able to close.

===== YOUR TURN — this is Claude talking (round 2) =====

===== YOUR HAT THIS PHASE =====
Come at this as a Delivery Lead — your lens is sequencing, dependencies, who owns what, and a realistic path to done. And bring the temperament of the User Advocate: keep a specific real user in the room and reject anything confusing, slow, or joyless for them. This is your stance for THIS phase only — lean into it and don't be a yes-man.
Continue the discussion: react to the new messages by name, defend or update your position, and push toward the best answer for this phase.
This is the last gate before code. Check that the prompt contract, product brief, design handoff, iOS architecture, tech specs, project plan, tasks, tests, and acceptance criteria all agree. If they do not, downgrade scope or name the exact blocker before build starts.

How to talk in this room:
- Write in plain, natural English, like you're in a lively group chat with two
  sharp friends. NO headings, NO numbered rubrics, NO 0-100 scores, NO
  bullet-point templates, NO sign-off line. Just talk like a person.
- Speak as exactly ONE person (yourself). Don't write the others' messages.
- Go deep and be specific. Make a real argument with concrete examples and think
  out loud. A couple of rich paragraphs, not a shallow blurb.
- React to what the others actually just said, by name (Codex / Claude /
  Gemini / any local model in the room / and the human if they chimed in).
  Quote or paraphrase their point, then build on it or push back on it.
- Genuinely try to CONVINCE the group of whatever you think is the single best
  idea right now — it does NOT have to be your own. If someone makes a better
  case, say so and change your mind out loud.
- Do NOT agree just to agree. If an idea is weak, explain why. Surface the real
  trade-offs and disagreements — that friction is the whole point.
- Make the decisions yourselves; don't punt to "the human."
response:
Codex, good to see we landed in the same place on the two unforced errors — CSV import flow missing from flows-json and the GapRegisterEntry.swift double-write — and I like your specific fix better than what I said, actually: "one owning lane for initial file creation and one consuming/handover task after first commit" is more precise than my vague "explicit ownership." Let's just make T-030 formally depend_on T-004 in addition to its existing dependencies, with a one-line acceptance criterion on T-004 saying the skeleton file must compile with placeholder entries so T-030 has something real to extend rather than overwrite. That's a five-minute fix to the tasks-json, not a debate.

But you didn't touch either of the two things I actually think are load-bearing, and I want to push on both again before we let this round close, because "nobody objected" isn't the same as "resolved."

On the requirements.json — here's the sharper version of my argument, because I think the coordinator undersold why timing matters here, not just existence. Even if I'm wrong and it turns out to exist somewhere I haven't seen, the current plan still has it being reconciled at T-033, which is the last task of a 33-task build spanning four lanes and probably a lot of wall-clock time. By the time T-033 runs, the rich context we have right now — every rationale, every rejected alternative, every "this maps to that requirement because of this specific decision" — will likely have been compressed or summarized multiple times over. Reconciling a 52-item requirement list against 33 tasks is exactly the kind of task that needs full context to do well, and we're proposing to do it at the point in the process with the least context remaining. That's backwards regardless of whether the file exists today. My ask isn't "prove it exists" — it's "produce it now, while every decision in this thread is fresh, as an actual artifact in the repo before T-001, and have T-033 do a much cheaper mechanical diff against something concrete instead of a first-time authoring pass under time pressure at the finish line." If Codex or anyone can point me to where the real 55-item list already lives, I'll happily downgrade this to "just move up the timing," but as of right now I've looked and what's adjacent to it in this thread is a mismatched R-001-through-R-033 flat scheme from what reads like an unrelated repair exercise, and that's not something I want to build against.

On the 30-day stats-history cap — I'll go further than I did last round: I think this is a real dropped requirement, not just an ambiguity, and here's why I'm confident rather than just suspicious. per_app_product_brief was explicit that Plus does exactly two things: removes the deck/card caps, and removes the 30-day stats window. Every other phase after that treats "Free/Plus gating" as one bundled must-have, which is exactly how a single differentiator can quietly ride along and get lost — tech_specs' DEC-tech_specs-009 gives us reminderHour/reminderMinute and the nil-vs-zero retentionRate typing, both good, but neither of those implements windowing. T-019 and T-020 are about proving the actor refresh works and computing forecast/history/retention at all — there's no acceptance criterion anywhere about a Free user's history view being truncated to 30 days versus a Plus user seeing everything. If this ships as built today, Plus has exactly one differentiator instead of two, and a user who pays for Plus specifically to see their six-month retention trend gets... the same screen as before. That's a monetization promise silently broken, and given how carefully this project protected "no dark patterns, no paywalling correctness" as a brand commitment, I don't think we get to be equally careless about the reverse — quietly not delivering what Plus is supposed to unlock. Concrete fix: add to T-020 that StatsComputationActor's history/forecast queries accept a windowing parameter sourced from PlanGate.isPlus (30 days for Free, unbounded for Plus), and add to T-021 an acceptance criterion that the stats screens visibly communicate when history is windowed (not just silently cut off — same honesty standard as everything else in this app).

The one thing from my last message that hasn't been picked up at all is the incremental-checkpoint idea, and I want to turn it from a vibe into an actual rule before we lock this, because I don't think either of you disagreed, you just didn't engage. Concretely: after T-011 (persistence tests green) and again after T-018 (review session + interruption tests green), whoever's running the build reports pass/fail on that slice before primary_ui/services_utilities/polish_resilience proceed into stats and CSV work. This costs nothing in scope — it's the same 33 tasks in the same order — it just means if the SM-2 package or the force-quit test is subtly wrong, we find out at task 11 or 18, not at task 33 after stats, CSV, reminders, and StoreKit have all been built on top of a shaky foundation. Given how much this project has staked on "provably right, not plausibly right," I think refusing to check our own proof partway through would be a strange place to get lazy.

So: two of the four items from last round are just mechanical fixes and I'd call those done. The requirements.json timing and the stats-cap gap are real, and I want either Codex to show me why I'm wrong or for us to lock both fixes into this phase's decisions before consensus. I don't think either one is a scope question — they're both "the plan we already agreed to has a hole in it," and the whole point of this gate is to not let holes like that survive into build.
